name: vitamins
title: Ray Peat on vitamins
question: Which vitamins did he consider most important?
description: What Ray Peat thought about vitamins: E as an antiestrogen, A and the thyroid, D and K with calcium, niacinamide and riboflavin in cell energy.
intro: For Ray Peat, vitamins were not mere supplements: he saw them as tied to hormones, to polyunsaturated fats and to the energy metabolism of cells. He held that vitamin E is above all an estrogen antagonist and not just an antioxidant [1], and that others such as A, D, K, niacinamide and riboflavin play a part in the thyroid, calcium and mitochondrial respiration [2][3][4].

sections.heading: Vitamin E as an estrogen antagonist
paragraphs: According to Peat, estrogen increases prostaglandin synthesis and activates enzymes such as COX and LOX, while vitamin E does the opposite [1]. He also held that estrogen releases enzymes from lysosomes and that vitamin E restrains that release [1].

Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) and prostaglandins act, in his view, as amplifiers of estrogen's effects. So he thought that if vitamin E protects against those fats, that alone would explain part of its antiestrogenic effect [1]. He added that it inhibits lipolysis and binds free fatty acids to inactivate them [1].

sections.heading: Vitamin E, fertility and polyunsaturated fats
paragraphs: Peat recounted that his thesis supervisor found in hamsters that extra vitamin E delayed middle-age infertility [1]. In his own experiments, vitamin E increased oxygen in the uterus and corrected the deficit caused by added estrogen or by old age [1]. According to him, estrogen reduces the oxygen available to the embryo and vitamin E increases it [1].

He pointed out that the need for vitamin E grows with age and with the amount of polyunsaturated fat in the diet. If those fats are carefully avoided, the need would be very low [5]. In rats, the amount needed to sustain pregnancy rose about 65-fold during the first year of life, and he believed estrogen raises the need for this vitamin [6].

sections.heading: Vitamin A, the thyroid and carotene
paragraphs: For Peat, vitamin A is the main cofactor that lets the thyroid turn cholesterol into steroid hormones [7]. He said the two work so closely together that a single protein, transthyretin, carries both, and that without thyroid vitamin A cannot be used [2].

In that context, he stated that carotene accumulates in steroid-producing tissues in hypothyroidism and competes with vitamin A, having an effect opposite to it [7][2]. He recalled that in the 1930s the red colour of those tissues was used to confirm death from hypothyroidism [2].

He also saw risks: he believed an excess of vitamin A inhibits the thyroid and that there is less risk of toxicity if vitamin E is taken at the same time [8]. Both its deficiency and a large excess release enzymes that dissolve cartilage [8].

sections.heading: Vitamins D and K and calcium control
paragraphs: According to Peat, vitamin D or a high calcium intake switches off parathyroid hormone, and that would prevent calcification of soft tissues [9]. He preferred sunlight to supplements [9]. When he spoke of vitamin D he meant cholecalciferol, not the 1,25-hydroxylated form, which in his view does the dirty work of the parathyroid [3]. He also held that vitamins D and K need carbon dioxide to handle calcium properly [10].

Of vitamin K2 he said it blocks the bone calcium loss caused by parathyroid hormone by preventing lactic acid production, and that it promotes the formation of bone proteins [11]. He stated that proteins C and S, which prevent abnormal clotting, cannot be made without it [12]. He added that much research supports it in hypertension, although in his view most doctors advise against it because of its reputation as a clotting vitamin [13]. He mentioned cases of high doses lowering blood pressure and said that in Japan doses far above dietary amounts were used without problems [12][14].

sections.heading: B vitamins: niacinamide and riboflavin
paragraphs: Peat favoured niacinamide because, according to him, it supplies energy to the mitochondrial system, reduces cell excitation and helps stabilise repair systems [4]. He explained that estrogen interferes with the formation of niacin from tryptophan [4]. He insisted on using the amide form and not nicotinic acid, because the flush it causes goes with the release of serotonin, histamine and toxic prostaglandins. He said 'no-flush' niacin releases the same things, only more slowly [15][16].

Of riboflavin (B2) he said it is a component of the mitochondrial respiratory enzymes and is easily destroyed by light [4]. He described the case of a child with nosebleeds and fits of rage that improved after a dose of riboflavin, and attributed it to an energy deficit [4]. On doses, he criticised the excess of the orthomolecular movement and preferred to try the smallest possible dose first, around five times the minimum daily requirement [16].

sections.heading: His criticism of the official view of vitamins
paragraphs: Peat held that in the 1940s vitamin E was redefined as an antioxidant, and that this change diverted attention from its relationship with estrogen and unsaturated fats [5][1]. According to him, the estrogen industry and the seed oil industry benefited from that idea, and research into its healing effects was held back for about 40 years [17][1].

He also stated that in the 1970s drug companies with synthetic forms of vitamin A promoted exaggerated stories about the toxicity of the natural one. That would have led many people to stop eating liver, which for him is an important source of vitamin E and vitamin K [1]. Even so, he acknowledged that vitamins A and D can be toxic in large amounts [18].

faq.q: Did Ray Peat consider vitamin E an antioxidant?
faq.a: According to Peat, that is a later redefinition: before the 1940s it was seen as an antiestrogen [5]. For him, its main role is to counter the effects of estrogen and polyunsaturated fats, not just to protect against oxidation [1].

faq.q: What link did Peat see between vitamin A and the thyroid?
faq.a: He held that the two work very closely together: they share a transport protein and, without thyroid, vitamin A cannot be used [2]. He also said that in hypothyroidism carotene accumulates and competes with vitamin A [7][2].

faq.q: Why did Peat prefer niacinamide to nicotinic acid?
faq.a: According to him, the flush from nicotinic acid comes with the release of serotonin, histamine and toxic prostaglandins, and 'no-flush' niacin releases the same things more slowly [15]. For Peat, the amide form avoids that [16].

faq.q: What did Peat think of vitamins D and K?
faq.a: He believed vitamin D, together with calcium, keeps parathyroid hormone low, and that K2 protects bone against its action [9][11]. He defended vitamin K against its reputation for promoting clots, because it is needed to make proteins C and S [12].
